summary: ASTRA-TWIN is a health-monitoring and decision-support digital twin for the seven-person crew of the International Space Station. ISS crews are not doctors, yet they are the first responders: the Crew Medical Officer gets about 15 hours of CMO-specific training, and in January 2026 crewmates were the first to respond to a medical event on the ISS. Each astronaut gets a personal twin, built on real NASA pre-flight blood data, that explains every body region in plain language and says what to do next. A shared Crew Deck shows who needs help and where, and guides the crew through an emergency. An Earth Twin looks 6–12 hours ahead and sends the flight surgeon's plan. The system never decides: it explains, warns and proposes, and the CMO decides. It runs offline and keeps psychological data private, following NASA-STD-3001.
details:
ASTRA-TWIN — a health digital twin for ISS crews

THE PROBLEM

On a long ISS mission, health problems usually start quietly: short sleep, dehydration, headaches, back pain. Sometimes they are sudden, like a crewmate collapsing. In both cases the first people to act are crewmates who are not physicians: the Crew Medical Officer (CMO) receives about 15 hours of CMO-specific training, and in January 2026 crewmates were the first to respond to a medical event on the ISS. NASA's own research says astronauts currently rely on real-time communication with ground-based medical providers and calls for a clinical decision support system. The ground is close on the ISS (seconds of delay), but S-band coverage is 90–95%, the first minutes belong to the crew, and seven people must coordinate across the station.

WHAT ASTRA-TWIN DOES

ASTRA-TWIN gives every astronaut a personal digital twin and gives the whole crew one shared view. It never decides on its own: it explains, warns and proposes, and the CMO or the ground decides.

1. Personal twin (3D body)

- A rotatable 3D anatomy model (NIH HuBMAP). Each region — head and brain, eyes, heart, lungs, blood and metabolism, bones and muscles, whole body — shows its status, what it means, what to do and how it is measured, in plain language and with sources.

- Each astronaut's baseline comes from real NASA pre-flight blood data, so a change is compared with the person's own normal.

- Each of the seven crew members has their own values, mission day and health story drawn from the most likely conditions in NASA's Integrated Medical Model (for example insomnia, headache, space motion sickness, skin rash, back pain, and pre-landing fluid loading).

- A "Today" strip with the day's tasks, fluid intake, check-in streak and the next measurement reminder.

2. Status levels that say who decides

L0 normal · L1 self-care advice (the astronaut) · L2 needs CMO approval · L3 CMO and flight surgeon · L4 emergency (the CMO acts on protocol; the ground is informed, not awaited). Every alert shows its threshold, evidence and source.

3. Daily check-in and reaction test

A two-minute, step-by-step check-in (mood, sleep, workload, crew climate, mission control, family, what helped you recharge, food) based on ISS behavioral-health practice, and a short reaction-time test with a personal best and a streak. The answers are private to the astronaut.

4. Crew Deck

A map of the ISS modules with every crew member's location and status color, a 3D view of the station, and each person's role. It never shows vital-sign detail or psychological data.

5. Emergency mode

When a crewmate collapses, the whole screen switches to an emergency view: who needs help and where, with an alarm. The system proposes roles (CMO-1 leads, CMO-2 assists, the nearest crew member fetches the life-support pack and defibrillator, the next one handles comms), and the CMO confirms or changes them. The crew follows the microgravity CPR checklist from Hinkelbein et al. 2020, with time-stamped steps, and sees an emergency card with allergies and current medication only.

6. Environment

Cabin CO2 on a gauge with NASA limit bands (1-hour average ≤ 3 mmHg) and its trend, and real ISS radiation data, including the September 2017 solar particle event, when the dose rule fires.

7. Earth Twin

A look-ahead slider to T+12 h over four forecasts: radiation dose from real ISS data, sleep debt from the astronaut's private check-ins (only they see it), fluids and core temperature. The flight surgeon's plan arrives with Accept or "Discuss at my next private conference", a forecast-vs-actual table makes forecast accuracy visible, and a "Next day" button shows how the twin changes over days.

8. Private support companion

A peer-support chat on a local language model that knows the astronaut's profile and last days. A safety gate and an output filter make sure it never gives a diagnosis or names a medication; in a crisis it points to the flight surgeon or the behavioral health provider. The conversation never leaves the station.

9. Roles and privacy

The same app can be viewed as an astronaut, the CMO, the ground (flight surgeon), the Crew Deck or the emergency view, and a server-side privacy filter decides what each one may see, following NASA-STD-3001 (private medical and psychological communications, V1 6002, 6003, 6011).

HOW IT WORKS

A Rust tool ingests NASA data into a local cache, so the app works without internet. A dependency-free Java 21 API runs the rules engine, the scenarios (crewmate collapse, CO2 rise, solar particle event), the twin forecasts, the privacy filter and a CSV telemetry stream that feeds simulated wearable readings, modelled on CSA's Bio-Monitor. A Tauri v2 desktop app shows the screens and also runs in a normal browser. Medication is only proposed from the 2023 ISS medication list and always needs CMO approval.

REAL AND SIMULATED DATA

Real: NASA OSDR pre-flight blood values (OSD-569, OSD-575, Inspiration4 crew), NASA Integrated Medical Model probabilities, NASA ISS TEPC dose data (CDAWeb) and NASA thresholds. Simulated: in-flight heart rate, SpO2, temperature, blood pressure and glucose, because no public dataset has them. Every value on screen is labelled real or simulated; crew callsigns are fictional.

SAFETY BY DESIGN

- A human always decides; each recommendation shows the data, threshold and source behind it, so the CMO can review it independently.

- Tiered alerts against alarm fatigue: only L4 takes over the screen; L1 is a quiet suggestion.

- Psychological data stays with the astronaut; the Crew Deck sees only a status color.

- Honest limits: this is a prototype, not a medical device, and forecast accuracy is not yet validated.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

We aim to help non-physician crews catch slow changes early, coordinate faster when a change is sudden, and understand their own health. The next step is testing in NASA's HERA analog habitat and comparing twin alerts with clinician judgement. The same design scales to the Moon and Mars, where the delay grows and the onboard twin must work more on its own.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

Two twins with different jobs (onboard: now; Earth: the next 12 hours), a real 3D anatomy instead of a chart, status levels that answer "who decides", and privacy built into the server, not just the screen.

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES

Frontend: Tauri v2, React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS 4, shadcn/ui, Motion, Recharts, three.js with react-three-fiber. Backend: Java 21 (no external dependencies), Rust (data ingest). Local model: Ollama with phi3.5. Demo video: Remotion. Runs on macOS and Ubuntu 24.

TEAM — HEAL ME OUT

Süleyman Erdem Şener, Mehmet Emin Yıldız and Duru Umman (Computer Engineering) and Mustafa Polat Güldağ (Nutrition and Dietetics). We joined software and health because on a long mission, care starts with the crew.

  • Link to Final Project: https://github.com/yldzemin/HealMeOut
  • Live demo: https://yldzemin.github.io/HealMeOut/
